title: Fill-in-the-Blank Phraseology — pilot batch
status: PILOT — 24 of a planned 36. Do not import to prod until the pattern is locked.
source: VictorOne English Phraseology Exam Briefing Package 1 (Part 2 — nine fill-in-the-blank tasks). Dialogues come from 'A Guide to VFR Phraseology' (Karmen Stumberger, MSc), the prep source the briefing names, except DLG-03 which is the briefing's own worked example. Every phrase used appears in the guide, but THREE TRANSCRIPTS ARE CONSTRUCTED rather than verbatim: DLG-04 merges the guide's two traffic exchanges (L777-781, two different aircraft) into one aircraft's dialogue; DLG-23 supplies a readback of 'maintain 2500 feet' that the guide's example omits although L322 makes a level instruction mandatory to read back; DLG-24 substitutes 'request full stop' from the phrase table (L1039) into the touch-and-go transcript.
authoring_notes:
TEMPLATE FORMAT: newline-separated lines, each prefixed [atc] or [pilot] for speaker styling (parse-dialog-display.ts). Blanks are bare {{n}} markers here; answers live only in `blanks`, and the importer composes the stored {{n|canonical;syn1;syn2}} token from that array so each answer has exactly one source of truth. Answers may not contain { } | ; (mig 125 CHECK — a student-leak guard).

BLANK-SHAPE RULE (the core authoring decision, user-directed 2026-08-11): shape the blank by where the answer comes from.
  * RECALLED — the answer appears nowhere on screen (e.g. 'request departure information', 'looking out'): give it ONE BLANK PER WORD and leave the LAST word of the phrase VISIBLE as the anchor ('{{0}} {{1}} information', '{{0}} out'). Anchoring on the final word is the house pattern — it is consistent across every recall blank in this file, and the validator enforces it as a RUN rule, not a line rule: a run of TWO OR MORE consecutive recall blanks must be followed, immediately and on the same line, by text containing a word character (punctuation alone does not count). A line rule would be wrong here — five lines across four questions are entirely blanks, which is exactly what the callsign-placement questions below require. Word count plus anchor turn blind recall into constrained recall. A student cannot guess a four-word phrase from a single empty box.
  * DERIVABLE — the controller already said it, or it is a direct transformation of what the controller said (e.g. 'runway 33', 'QNH 1014', 'lining up and waiting' from 'line up and wait'): use ONE PHRASE BLANK. Splitting these would leak the answer, and on a readback-selection question it would reveal WHICH items to pick, destroying the test.
This diverges deliberately from the real exam, whose own example brackets whole phrases ('[descending to 2500 feet]'). The product is TRAINING, so learnability wins; revisit if the timed mock exam is built.

CALLSIGN PLACEMENT — THE SOURCE'S RULE (corrected 2026-08-11 after a faithfulness audit): callsign at the FRONT by default; at the END when the pilot is READING BACK an instruction or important information, or ACKNOWLEDGING one (wilco / roger / looking out). Guide L535-537 verbatim: 'the message is normally prefixed with the aircraft call sign. However, when the pilot needs to read back an instruction or important information, he places the call sign at the end of the message.' Corroborated at L330-331 and by the briefing ('placing the callsign at the end of the readback').

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS READBACK, NOT RESPONSE. An earlier revision taught 'front if you initiate, end if you respond'. That is right wherever a response IS a readback — most of the time — and wrong where it is not: a pilot answering 'report position' front-places (L1329, L1383), and 'S-AA, traffic in sight' (L781) front-places because reporting something newly seen reads nothing back. That revision declared L781 a source typo to protect the inferred rule. It is NOT a typo; the guide is self-consistent, and L970 shows the same phrase END-placed when bundled into an acknowledgement. Never declare a source line erroneous to preserve a rule you inferred — re-read the prose first.

VERIFIED COUNT (L86-L1028, the range every question draws from): 62 fixed-wing pilot transmissions, 33 front-placed and 29 end-placed, ZERO violations of the rule above. The book's two genuine violations sit outside that range (L1446, L1545 — requests carrying an end-placed callsign). A previously recorded '38/18/1' count was not reproducible under any scope and is withdrawn.

HOW TO TEST PLACEMENT: only on a pilot line carrying EXACTLY TWO blanks, where the student decides which holds the callsign. If the callsign's slot is fixed by surrounding text, the template has already answered the question.

DO NOT TEST: whether WIND is read back — the guide reads it back at Maribor take-off but omits it at Ljubljana take-off and at the S-MN landing clearance. Both were candidate questions and both were cut. Only test what the source states as a rule, never a pattern inferred across examples.

EVERY BLANK CARRIES `shape`: 'recall' (answer appears nowhere on screen) or 'derivable' (the controller said it, or it is a direct transformation of what he said). The validator is scripts/dialog-fill-content.ts (assertDialogFillAuthoring), run over every question in this file by scripts/dialog-fill-content.test.ts and again by the importer before any write. It asserts four rules: R1 every blank carries a shape; R2 a recall CANONICAL is a single word — SYNONYMS ARE EXEMPT, and several single-word recall answers legitimately carry multi-word synonyms (wilco accepts 'will report runway vacated'); R3 a recall canonical never appears in the visible template, compared under normalize_answer semantics; R4 the run-anchor rule above. Single-word standard phrases (wilco) are recall but need no split, and a run of one never engages R4. This is what makes the rule checkable rather than a convention that erodes over 30 questions.
grading_notes: Graded per blank against canonical + synonyms with normalize_answer (lowercase, strips punctuation, hyphen/underscore to space, collapses whitespace) — so case, commas, hyphens and the European decimal comma are already free ('118.0' and '118,0' both normalize to '1180'). Synonym policy: (a) numbers take digit AND spoken forms; (b) verbs take both aspects where a pilot could reasonably write either; (c) every abbreviated callsign accepts the run-together spelling, since the normalizer maps 'S-AA' to 's aa' and NOT to 'saa'. Fixed standard phrases stay STRICT — they are the exact terms under test. A full callsign is never a synonym for its abbreviated form, or the abbreviation rule becomes untestable.

questions.prompt: Engine start-up at Portoroz. Complete the pilot's request, then the readback of the departure information. Read the items back in the order the controller gave them.
questions.template:
[pilot] Portoroz Tower S5-DAA, radio check 115,15
[atc] S5-DAA Portoroz Tower, read you 5
[pilot] S5-DAA, {{0}} {{1}} information
[atc] S-AA, runway 33, wind 090 degrees 6 knots, QNH 1014, temperature 5, dew point 3, clouds scattered at 2000 feet
[pilot] {{2}}, {{3}}, S-AA

blanks.rule: Basic phrases — recalled, so split per word with 'information' left as the anchor.
Basic phrases — second word of the standard pre-departure request.
Items to be read back — runway in use. Derivable from the controller's transmission, so one phrase blank.
Items to be read back — altimeter setting. Only the QNH is read back from a met report.

questions.explanation: **The controller passed six items — you read back two.** The departure information carries runway, wind, QNH, temperature, dew point and cloud, but only two sit on the mandatory readback list: the **runway in use** and the **altimeter setting**. Wind, temperature, dew point and cloud are information, not clearance, and are not read back at all. Read them back **in the order given** — the guide calls that normally best rather than absolute — and note the callsign, given here, sits at the **end**: this is a readback, and a readback closes with the callsign.

questions.prompt: Taxi instructions at Maribor. Complete the pilot's readback.

blanks.rule: Use of wilco — an instruction to report later is acknowledged, not read back. The guide uses 'wilco' and 'will report ...' interchangeably here, so both are accepted.
Callsign placement — a readback ends with the callsign; abbreviated because ATC abbreviated first.

questions.explanation: **WILCO means 'I understand your message and will comply with it'.** Everything on the mandatory readback list has already come back — the runway and the QNH — along with the taxi limit, which is *not* on that list but is always read back so the controller knows where you will stop. What remains is *report ready for departure*, an instruction to act later, so it takes **wilco** (the guide also accepts *will report ready for departure*). The boundary matters: wilco is **never a substitute** for reading back a clearance, a runway instruction or an altimeter setting.

questions.prompt: Approaching Portoroz. Complete the pilot's two transmissions — note carefully which form of the callsign each one takes.
questions.template:
[pilot] Portoroz Approach S5-ABC
[atc] S5-ABC Portoroz Approach, go ahead
[pilot] {{0}}, overhead PE1, 3500 feet, for approach
[atc] S-BC, QNH 1025, descend to 2500 feet, next report overhead PE2
[pilot] QNH 1025, {{1}}, {{2}}, {{3}}

blanks.rule: Abbreviated callsigns — the pilot may NOT abbreviate until ATC has.

synonyms: descending to two thousand five hundred feet
descending to two thousand five hundred
blanks.rule: Items to be read back — level instruction. Derivable from the controller's words, so one phrase blank.
Use of wilco — an instruction to report later is acknowledged, not read back. The guide uses 'wilco' and 'will report ...' interchangeably here, so both are accepted.
Abbreviated callsigns — permitted now, because ATC abbreviated in the previous transmission.

questions.explanation: **The same slot takes two different answers in one exchange, and the controller decides which.** In the third line the pilot must still say the full **S5-ABC**: the controller has used the full callsign throughout, and a pilot may only use the shortened form *once addressed in that manner by the controller*. In the last line **S-BC** is correct — and required — because the controller abbreviated first. The readback follows the usual rules: QNH and *descending to 2500 feet* are both mandatory, *next report overhead PE2* takes **wilco**, and the callsign closes the message.

questions.prompt: Traffic information en route. The pilot acknowledges traffic he cannot yet see, then reports it once he has located it. Complete both transmissions.
questions.template:
[atc] S-AB, light aircraft 11 o'clock, crossing left to right at 4500 feet
[pilot] {{0}} out, S-AB
[pilot] S-AB, {{1}} {{2}} sight

blanks.rule: Basic phrases — acknowledging traffic not yet sighted; 'out' anchors the phrase.
Basic phrases — reporting the traffic located; 'sight' anchors the phrase.
Basic phrases — middle word of the standard sighting report.

questions.explanation: **Two standard phrases, and the callsign moves between them.** Until you have located the other aircraft you answer **looking out**; once you have it visually you report **traffic in sight**. If you cannot find it at all the phrase is **negative contact** — never silence, because the controller needs to know you are still searching. Watch the callsign: *looking out* acknowledges what the controller just told you, so it goes **last**; *traffic in sight* reports something new rather than reading anything back, so it goes **first**. The trigger for end-placement is reading back or acknowledging — not merely answering.

questions.prompt: Ready to depart from Maribor. Complete the pilot's report and the acknowledgement that follows.
questions.template:
[pilot] S-BS, {{0}} {{1}} departure
[atc] S-BS, line up and wait
[pilot] {{2}}, S-BS

blanks.rule: Basic phrases — recalled, so split per word with 'departure' as the anchor.
Basic phrases — second word of the standard report.
Acknowledgement by transformation — derivable from the controller's instruction, so one phrase blank.

questions.explanation: **An action instruction comes back as the action, not as an echo.** The controller says *line up and wait*; the pilot answers **lining up and waiting** — present participle, because you are describing what you are now doing. The same shape appears throughout: *taxi to holding point A* becomes *taxiing*, *vacate right* becomes *vacating*. This applies to action verbs; a clearance comes back unchanged (*runway 14 cleared for take-off*). Note also that **line up is not a take-off clearance** — it permits you onto the runway and nothing more. The word *take-off* is reserved for the clearance and its cancellation; at all other times say *departure* or *airborne*.

questions.prompt: Lined up at Ljubljana when the controller stops the departure. Complete the pilot's acknowledgement.
questions.template:
[atc] S-AT, line up runway 12, cleared for take-off, wind 090 degrees 6 knots, after departure turn right to S3, climb to 2500 feet
[pilot] line up runway 12, cleared for take-off, turn right to S3, climb to 2500 feet, S-AT
[atc] S-AT, hold position, I say again, hold position, obstacle on runway 12
[pilot] {{0}} position, S-AT

blanks.rule: Acknowledgement by transformation — 'position' is left visible as the anchor, so only the transformed verb is tested.

questions.explanation: **HOLD POSITION is a safety instruction and it has one correct answer: holding position.** The controller repeats it — *I say again* — because an aircraft rolling onto an occupied runway is the accident this phrase exists to prevent. Answer immediately, in the participle form, so the controller hears that you are complying. The take-off readback above is shown rather than tested; note it is a brief one, and the guide elsewhere reads the departure instructions back in full.

questions.prompt: En route, approaching Ljubljana. Complete the pilot's readback of the frequency change.
questions.template:
[pilot] S-BS, 3 minutes before NE
[atc] S-BS, contact Ljubljana tower 118.0
[pilot] {{0}}, S-BS

blanks.rule: Readback of a frequency — the number only, not the unit name.

questions.explanation: **Read back the frequency, not the station.** The controller names both the unit and the number; only the number is read back, then the callsign. Reading back *Ljubljana tower 118.0* is not wrong so much as wasteful — frequency changes are short by design, because you are about to leave this frequency and any delay is time nobody is listening to you. The decimal separator does not matter to the grader: **118.0** and **118,0** are treated identically, and both spellings appear in the source.

questions.prompt: On base at Portoroz. Complete the pilot's readback of the landing clearance.
questions.template:
[pilot] S-MN, base
[atc] S-MN, runway 33, cleared to land, wind 300 degrees, 8 knots gusting at 12
[pilot] {{0}}, {{1}}, S-MN

blanks.rule: Items to be read back — runway instruction.
Items to be read back — a clearance to land on a runway.

questions.explanation: **A landing clearance must be read back in full; the wind that comes with it need not be.** Clearances to land on, take off from, enter, cross or backtrack a runway are all on the mandatory list — this is the readback that stops two aircraft being cleared onto the same strip of asphalt. The wind is passed so you can judge the approach, not because it needs confirming. Finish with the callsign, abbreviated here because the controller abbreviated earlier in the circuit.

questions.prompt: En route to Novo mesto, leaving controlled airspace. Complete the pilot's readback.

synonyms: will report before changing to local frequency
blanks.rule: Use of wilco — an instruction to report later is acknowledged, not read back. The guide uses 'wilco' and 'will report ...' interchangeably here, so both are accepted.
Callsign placement — a readback ends with the callsign; abbreviated because ATC abbreviated first.

questions.explanation: **Three parts, three different treatments, in one transmission.** The **QNH** is an altimeter setting, so it is read back verbatim. *Continue visually to Novo mesto* is an instruction you act on now, so it comes back transformed — **continuing**. *Report before changing to local frequency* is an instruction for later, so it takes **wilco**. Learning to sort a controller's message into those three buckets — read back, transform, acknowledge — is most of Part 2.

questions.prompt: Straight-in approach to Ljubljana. Complete the callsign at the end of each pilot transmission.

blanks.rule: Abbreviated callsigns — ATC is still using the full callsign, so the pilot must too.
Abbreviated callsigns — ATC abbreviated in the previous transmission, so the pilot may now.

questions.explanation: **One approach, two callsigns, and you do not choose either — the controller does.** Read the controller's line immediately above each blank and copy the form used there. In the first readback the tower is still saying *S5-DJP*, so the pilot must answer in full. By the landing clearance the tower has moved to *S-JP*, and only then may the pilot shorten it. The rule is one-directional: the controller abbreviates first, the pilot follows. Note in passing what each readback keeps — the approach clearance, the runway, the QNH — and what it drops: the wind, both times.

questions.prompt: Joining the circuit at Portoroz. Complete the pilot's readback of the joining instructions, taking the items in the order the controller gave them.

blanks.rule: Items to be read back — altimeter setting.
Items to be read back — runway in use.
Use of wilco — an instruction to report later is acknowledged, not read back. The guide uses 'wilco' and 'will report ...' interchangeably here, so both are accepted.
Abbreviated callsigns — ATC has used the FULL callsign, so the pilot may not shorten it yet.

questions.explanation: **This one puts all four Part 2 skills in a single transmission.** The **QNH** and the **runway in use** are read back because both are on the mandatory list. The two continuation instructions come back transformed — *continuing*, *descending*. *Report runway in sight* takes **wilco**. And the callsign stays **full**: the controller opened with *S5-DMN* and has not abbreviated, so neither may you — a detail that is easy to lose at the end of a long readback, which is exactly where it is tested.

questions.prompt: Position report to Ljubljana Information. Complete the pilot's acknowledgement.
questions.template:
[pilot] Ljubljana Information S5-DEW
[atc] S5-DEW Ljubljana Information
[pilot] S5-DEW overhead Velike Lasce at 24, passing 4500 feet, climbing to 6500 feet, estimating ILB at 40, PE1 next
[atc] S-EW report three minutes before PE1
[pilot] {{0}}, {{1}}

synonyms: will report three minutes before PE1
blanks.rule: Use of wilco — an instruction to report later is acknowledged, not read back. The guide uses 'wilco' and 'will report ...' interchangeably here, so both are accepted.
Callsign placement — this READS BACK or acknowledges, so the callsign goes at the end.

questions.explanation: **Two blanks, and you decide which one holds the callsign.** *Report three minutes before PE1* is an instruction to act later, so it takes **wilco** — or *will report three minutes before PE1*; the guide uses both. Nothing here is on the mandatory readback list. Because this transmission acknowledges what the controller said, the callsign goes **last**. Compare the pilot's position report above it: that one reads nothing back, so the callsign came **first**.

questions.prompt: Transponder code assignment. Complete the pilot's readback.
questions.template:
[atc] S-AA, advise transponder capability
[pilot] transponder Charlie, S-AA
[atc] S-AA, squawk 6503
[pilot] {{0}}, {{1}}

blanks.rule: Items to be read back — SSR code.
Callsign placement — this READS BACK or acknowledges, so the callsign goes at the end.

questions.explanation: **An SSR code is on the mandatory readback list, and it is there for a reason.** A mis-set transponder makes you the wrong aircraft on the controller's screen, or invisible. Read the code back digit by digit — except codes of whole thousands, which are spoken as thousands. Remember the reserved codes: **7700** emergency, **7600** radio failure, **7500** unlawful interference, and **2000** when none has been assigned. The callsign goes last because you are reading back.

questions.prompt: Conditional line-up at Ljubljana. Complete the pilot's readback of the conditional clearance.
questions.template:
[atc] S5-DBS, report Seneca on final in sight
[pilot] Seneca in sight, S5-DBS
[atc] S5-DBS, behind the landing Seneca, line up behind
[pilot] {{0}}, {{1}}, S5-DBS

blanks.rule: Conditional clearance — the CONDITION must be repeated, not just the clearance.
Conditional clearance — the clearance itself follows the condition.

questions.explanation: **A conditional clearance is read back with its condition, and the condition comes first.** *Behind the landing Seneca* is not scene-setting — it is what makes the line-up safe, and repeating it proves you have identified the right aircraft. That is why the controller asked you to report the Seneca in sight first: for movements affecting an active runway, a conditional clearance may only be given when both controller and pilot can see the aircraft concerned. Note this readback echoes the clearance as issued rather than transforming it — *line up behind*, not *lining up behind* — though both are accepted here.

questions.prompt: Conditional landing clearance. Complete the pilot's readback.
questions.template:
[atc] S-GI, report departing Cessna in sight
[pilot] Cessna in sight, S-GI
[atc] S-GI, after departing Cessna has passed, runway 14, cleared to land, wind calm
[pilot] {{0}}, {{1}}, {{2}}, S-GI

synonyms: after the departing Cessna has passed
blanks.rule: Conditional clearance — the condition is repeated first.
Items to be read back — runway instruction.
Items to be read back — a landing clearance.

questions.explanation: **Condition, runway, clearance — and nothing else.** The controller also passed *wind calm*; the wind is information for flying the approach and is not read back. What must come back is the condition that the departing Cessna has passed, the runway, and the clearance itself. Drop the condition from your readback and you have told the controller you are cleared to land now, which is not what he said.

questions.prompt: The pilot asks Maribor Tower for the present weather. Complete the readback.

blanks.rule: Items to be read back — altimeter setting. It is the ONLY item read back from a weather report.
Callsign placement and form — a readback ends with the callsign, and it stays FULL because ATC has not abbreviated.

questions.explanation: **Five items of weather, one readback.** Wind, cloud, temperature and dew point are all information you use and none of them is confirmed back — only the **QNH**, because an altimeter setting you have misheard puts you at the wrong height. This is the purest form of the Part 2 selection skill: the shorter your readback, the better you have understood the rule. Note the callsign stays **full**: the tower said *S5-DBS*, so you may not shorten it.

questions.prompt: Landing clearance with a braking-action warning. Read back the clearance, then acknowledge the warning.
questions.template:
[atc] S5-DSC, runway 30 cleared to land, just landed Cessna reported braking action poor
[pilot] runway 30 {{0}}, {{1}}, S5-DSC

blanks.rule: Items to be read back — a landing clearance. 'runway 30' is left visible so the split is unambiguous.
Acknowledgement — ROGER receipts information that needs no readback.

questions.explanation: **ROGER and WILCO are not interchangeable.** *Roger* means 'I have received all of your last transmission'; *wilco* means 'I understand your message and will comply with it'. The braking-action report is information — there is nothing to comply with and nothing to read back — so it takes **roger**. The landing clearance beside it is on the mandatory list and must come back in full. Using *wilco* for information, or *roger* for a clearance, are the two classic errors here. Strictly the guide allows the callsign alone to acknowledge; *roger* makes it explicit.

questions.prompt: On short final when the controller sends you around. Complete the pilot's reply.
questions.template:
[atc] S-JP, go around, vehicle on the runway
[pilot] {{0}} around, S-JP

blanks.rule: Acknowledgement by transformation — 'around' is left visible as the anchor.

questions.explanation: **GO AROUND becomes GOING AROUND, and it is said immediately.** Like *hold position*, this is an instruction where the controller needs to hear that you are acting, not merely listening — so it comes back in the participle. Fly the aeroplane first and transmit second. If you decide to go around yourself, the same phrase announces it: **going around**. Unless told otherwise you then continue into the traffic circuit.

questions.prompt: A touch-and-go at Ljubljana. Three pilot transmissions — decide where the callsign belongs in each.

blanks.rule: Acknowledgement — responding to 'report final'.
Callsign placement — this READS BACK or acknowledges, so the callsign goes at the end.
Callsign placement — this reports something new rather than reading anything back, so the callsign goes in front.

synonyms: runway one four cleared touch and go
runway 14 cleared for touch and go
blanks.rule: Items to be read back — a runway clearance.
Callsign placement — this READS BACK or acknowledges, so the callsign goes at the end.

questions.explanation: **The same callsign, three times, in two different places — and the aircraft never changed.** The first and third transmissions ACKNOWLEDGE or READ BACK what the controller said, so the callsign closes them. The middle one reports something new — you are on final, and nothing is being read back — so the callsign opens it. That is the rule: **front by default, last when you read back or acknowledge**. Either *will report final* or *wilco* is correct for the first blank; the guide uses both. Note the wind is not read back, and *expect touch-and-go* is not yet a clearance — the clearance is the last transmission.

questions.prompt: After landing at Portoroz. Complete the pilot's readback.
questions.template:
[atc] S-MN, vacate right, report runway vacated, continue to general aviation apron via taxiways A and T
[pilot] {{0}}, continuing to general aviation apron via taxiways A and T, {{1}}, S-MN

blanks.rule: Acknowledgement by transformation — the instruction comes back as the action.
Use of wilco — an instruction to report later is acknowledged, not read back. The guide uses 'wilco' and 'will report ...' interchangeably here, so both are accepted.

questions.explanation: **Three instructions, three treatments, one transmission.** *Vacate right* and *continue to the apron* are things you are doing now, so they come back transformed — **vacating**, **continuing**. *Report runway vacated* is for later, so it takes **wilco**. You are still on a live runway until you report vacated, which is why that report matters and why the controller asked for it separately.

questions.prompt: Cloud ahead en route. Complete the pilot's transmission telling the controller and requesting a turn.
questions.template: [pilot] S5-DAA, {{0}} to maintain VMC due clouds, request turn left to Ptuj

blanks.rule: Basic phrases — the standard way to state you cannot comply; 'to maintain VMC' anchors it.

questions.explanation: **UNABLE is the word that starts the conversation early.** A VFR pilot who cannot stay in visual conditions has a developing problem, and the phrase that says so is *unable to maintain VMC*. Say it while you still have options — a turn, a descent, a diversion — rather than after the cloud has closed in. Note the callsign is at the **front**: you are initiating this transmission, not answering one.

questions.prompt: Lesce is in sight — not the planned destination — and the pilot is leaving the information frequency before landing. Complete the transmission.
questions.template: [pilot] Ljubljana Information S5-DJJ, airport Lesce in sight, changing to local frequency, {{0}} {{1}} flight plan

blanks.rule: Basic phrases — recalled, so split per word with 'flight plan' as the anchor.
Basic phrases — second word of the standard request.

questions.explanation: **A flight plan left open triggers a search.** When you land at an aerodrome that is not your planned destination, you must close the plan yourself — by radio before landing, as here, or by telephone afterwards — to avoid unnecessary search and rescue activity. The station confirms with a time: *flight plan closed at 40*. Note the shape of an initiating call: station name, then your callsign, then the message.

questions.prompt: Crossing controlled airspace near Maribor. Complete the pilot's position report on reaching the boundary point.
questions.template:
[atc] S-AS, maintain 2500 feet, report over ME1
[pilot] maintaining 2500 feet, wilco, S-AS
[pilot] {{0}}, {{1}}, 2500 feet

blanks.rule: Callsign placement — this reports something new rather than reading anything back, so the callsign goes in front.
Position report — the reporting point the controller asked for.

questions.explanation: **Compare the two pilot transmissions.** The first READS BACK the level instruction and acknowledges the reporting instruction, so it ends with the callsign. The second reports a new fact — you are over ME1 — and reads nothing back, so it opens with the callsign. That is the test: not whether you are answering, but whether you are reading something back. (The guide's own transcript omits the readback line shown here; a level instruction is on the mandatory list, so it is supplied.)

questions.prompt: Finishing a training detail in the circuit. Complete the pilot's request.
questions.template:
[pilot] S-AT, downwind, {{0}} {{1}} stop
[atc] S-AT, report final runway 14

blanks.rule: Basic phrases — recalled, so split per word with 'stop' as the anchor.
Basic phrases — naming which of the three training options you want.

questions.explanation: **Three requests, three different intentions, and the controller plans the circuit around which one you use.** *Touch-and-go* means you land and take off again without stopping; *stop-and-go* means you land, come to a full stop, then depart; **full stop** means the training detail is over. Say which you want while still downwind so the sequence can be arranged. The callsign is in front because you are reporting your position and making a request — nothing is being read back.
